title: dialled in
vibe: Said with admiration when someone is in peak focus — totally locked in and performing at their best.
literal_fail: 'Marcado en' sounds like you called someone. Doesn't exist as a phrase in Spanish.

examples.context: Your mate is playing pool and sinking every shot.
examples.note: 'In their sauce' — fully in their element, completely switched on.

examples.context: A footballer who can't put a foot wrong tonight.
examples.note: Enchufado literally means plugged in — the Spanish metaphor for being switched on and firing.

examples.context: A colleague nailing every presentation this week.
examples.note: On a roll — might be the closest for sustained peak performance.

examples.context: A gamer in the zone, not missing a beat.
examples.es: Está concentradísimo / está en modo bestia.
examples.note: 'Beast mode' has made it into Spanish slang among younger speakers.

examples.context: A musician who played a flawless set.
examples.note: When the performance was inspired rather than just focused — elevated.

title: and for your next trick
vibe: Dry, sardonic — said after someone has done something impressively stupid or unbelievably clumsy.
literal_fail: 'Y para tu próximo truco' is technically understandable but reads as a literal magic show announcement.

examples.context: Someone spills their drink then immediately knocks something else over.
examples.es: ¿Y ahora qué vas a hacer, mago?
examples.note: 'And what are you going to do now, wizard?' — the sarcasm lands perfectly in Spanish.

examples.context: Your mate breaks two things in a row doing DIY.
examples.note: 'Keep it up, champion' — affectionate sarcasm that Spanish speakers use constantly.

examples.context: A colleague makes a mess of one thing and immediately starts another.
examples.note: Rhetorical exhaustion — what else could you possibly manage to do?

examples.context: Someone trips, recovers, then immediately trips again.
examples.note: You're quite the spectacle — show has a slightly theatrical, sarcastic edge here.

examples.context: After a spectacular blunder at work.
examples.note: Award for merit — delivered completely deadpan, it lands like a punch.

title: what part of you could possibly have thought that was a good idea
vibe: Exasperated disbelief — usually affectionate, said when someone has done something spectacularly ill-conceived.
literal_fail: A direct translation exists but at 20 words it's too long to feel natural. Spanish condenses disbelief.

examples.context: Your friend tried to fix the boiler themselves and flooded the kitchen.
examples.note: 'What were you thinking?' — the classic. Short, sharp, universal.

examples.context: Someone booked a non-refundable flight before checking if they had work.
examples.note: 'How did that occur to you?' — genuinely baffled, not angry. Very Spanish.

examples.context: A teenager dyed their hair green before a job interview.
examples.note: 'What kind of head do you have?' — questioning the very brain involved in the decision.

examples.context: Someone tried to carry twenty bags in one trip and dropped everything.
examples.note: Soft, slightly amused exasperation. Literally 'well good, what are you doing?'

examples.context: A mate sent a voice note to the wrong person.
examples.note: 'You don't do that' — the understated Spanish version of total incredulity.

title: that's just poetry
vibe: Said when something is so perfectly done, so elegantly constructed, or so beautifully executed that it transcends ordinary praise.
literal_fail: 'Eso es poesía pura' works but sounds like you're reviewing a book. Needs to feel spontaneous.

examples.context: A footballer bends a free kick into the top corner.
examples.es: Eso no tiene nombre. Es un golazo de antología.
examples.note: A goal for the history books — antología is the Spanish way of saying something is all-time.

examples.context: A chef produces a dish that's visually and tastefully perfect.
examples.es: Eso es una obra de arte.
examples.note: A work of art — the most natural Spanish expression for something aesthetically perfect.

examples.context: A writer produces a perfectly constructed sentence.
examples.note: Pure literature — close to 'that's just poetry' in register and tone.

examples.context: A friend delivers the perfect comeback at the perfect moment.
examples.note: 'That was gold' — the Spanish equivalent for something perfectly timed and beautiful.

examples.context: A musician improvises something breathtaking.
examples.es: Eso se lo lleva el viento.
examples.note: Gone with the wind — something so fleeting and perfect it can't be replicated.

title: elementary my dear
vibe: Playfully smug — said when pointing out something that should have been obvious, with mock Sherlock energy.
literal_fail: 'Elemental, querido mío' actually exists in Spanish — it's the direct translation and everyone knows it from Sherlock Holmes. It works.

examples.context: You solve a puzzle your friend has been stuck on for ten minutes.
examples.note: This one actually translates — it entered Spanish directly from Holmes. Use it freely.

examples.context: Explaining why of course the restaurant was closed on Monday.
examples.note: 'It was in the drawer' — obvious, should have been clear. Stronger than elemental.

examples.context: Pointing out the obvious flaw in a plan someone spent hours on.
examples.note: Completely obvious. The -ísimo makes it gently withering.

examples.context: After deducing where your friend left their phone.
examples.note: 'Two plus two' — the Spanish way of saying it's simple maths, completely obvious.

examples.context: Working out why the plan failed from the start.
examples.note: It was staring you in the face — 'jumped to the eyes.' Vivid and very Spanish.

title: I'm not being funny but
vibe: British preamble to something that is slightly rude, contentious, or brutally honest — softens the blow just enough to say it anyway.
literal_fail: 'No estoy siendo gracioso pero' sounds like you're worried people think you're joking. Doesn't land.

examples.context: Telling a friend their new haircut doesn't suit them.
examples.es: Mira, te lo digo con todo el cariño del mundo, pero...
examples.note: 'I say this with all the love in the world, but...' — the standard Spanish setup for uncomfortable honesty.

examples.context: Pointing out that a colleague's plan won't work.
examples.es: Oye, sin ánimo de ofender, pero...
examples.note: 'No offence intended, but...' — more formal but widely used.

examples.context: Saying something slightly controversial at a family dinner.
examples.es: A ver, y esto que no salga de aquí, pero...
examples.note: This stays between us, but... — adds conspiratorial flavour to the delivery.

examples.context: Telling a mate his girlfriend is trouble.
examples.note: 'I'm telling you as a friend' — the classic Spanish preamble before saying something they might not want to hear.

examples.context: Complaining about a situation at work.
examples.es: No me malinterpretes, pero esto ya es demasiado.
examples.note: Don't get me wrong, but this is too much — closer in structure to the English original.

title: it does what it says on the tin
vibe: Approving understatement — exactly what it promised, no more, no less. Unpretentious and reliable.
literal_fail: 'Hace lo que pone en el bote' technically works as a reference but Spanish doesn't have the same advertising origin.

examples.context: A cheap, basic hotel that was clean and comfortable.
examples.note: It fulfilled its purpose — functional, no frills, did its job.

examples.context: A tool that works exactly as described.
examples.es: Es lo que es, sin más.
examples.note: 'It is what it is, nothing more' — same energy of unpretentious reliability.

examples.context: A film that delivered exactly the action it promised.
examples.es: Ni más ni menos, lo que te esperabas.
examples.note: Exactly what you expected, nothing more or less — the Spanish equivalent of the sentiment.

examples.context: A restaurant that serves straightforward, honest food.
examples.note: Honest cooking, no tricks — a phrase used by food writers that captures the same ethos.

examples.context: Software that just works, no fuss.
examples.note: 'It works, full stop' — the most concise Spanish way to say something does exactly what it should.

title: taking the mickey
vibe: British for teasing, mocking, or taking the piss — can be affectionate or genuinely accusatory.
literal_fail: There is no Mickey in Spanish. 'Tomar el pelo' (pull someone's hair) is the near-perfect equivalent.

examples.context: A mate winds you up about your terrible parking.
examples.note: 'He's pulling my leg/hair' — tomar el pelo is the exact Spanish equivalent. Learn it.

examples.context: A shop charges an outrageous price for something basic.
examples.es: Esto es una tomadura de pelo.
examples.note: The noun form — a mickey-take, a rip-off. Very common in consumer complaints.

examples.context: Someone makes fun of how long you spent getting ready.
examples.note: Are you having me on? — also means 'are you taking the mickey?' Extremely common.

examples.context: A comedian roasts someone affectionately.
examples.note: Vacilar = to tease, wind up, take the mickey. Very common in Spain.

examples.context: A colleague questions if the timeline on a project is serious.
examples.note: 'Is this serious or what?' — disbelief that bleeds into feeling mocked.

title: goes without saying
vibe: Said before stating something obvious — paradoxically said even though it apparently goes without saying.
literal_fail: 'Va sin decir' doesn't exist in Spanish. The equivalent is a completely different phrase.

examples.context: Reminding someone that of course they're invited.
examples.note: 'It goes without saying' — huelga decir is the formal equivalent. Huelga = it strikes (as unnecessary).

examples.context: Pointing out that of course quality costs more.
examples.es: Ni que decir tiene que la calidad tiene un precio.
examples.note: 'It goes without saying that quality has a price' — ni que decir tiene is the most natural version.

examples.context: Before stating an obvious consequence.
examples.note: It's clear that... — simpler but widely used when something is assumed.

examples.context: Adding a caveat that's obviously understood.
examples.es: Por supuesto, sin que haga falta decirlo...
examples.note: Of course, without needing to say it... — verbose but correct.

examples.context: Reaffirming a given.
examples.note: 'It's in the drawer' — completely obvious, doesn't need to be said.

title: as it happens
vibe: Conversational pivot — used to introduce a convenient coincidence or a relevant fact, often with mild surprise.
literal_fail: 'Como sucede' is too literal and sounds like a documentary. The Spanish has a completely different feel.

examples.context: You mention you need a plumber and your friend happens to be one.
examples.note: 'Well it turns out that...' — resultar is the go-to verb for convenient coincidences in Spanish.

examples.context: Someone asks if you've met the new boss and you have.
examples.es: Pues mira, da la casualidad de que sí.
examples.note: As it happens, yes — da la casualidad is the closest direct equivalent to 'as it happens.'

examples.context: Revealing you already knew the answer all along.
examples.note: Casualmente = coincidentally, as it happens — slightly formal but very natural.

examples.context: Bringing up a relevant fact at exactly the right moment.
examples.note: 'How curious that you mention it' — cues the relevant information with mild surprise.

examples.context: A serendipitous connection at a party.
examples.note: Well what a coincidence — warm, slightly amused. Very natural spoken Spanish.

title: the penny's dropped
vibe: That moment when someone finally understands something they've been struggling with — the light comes on.
literal_fail: Coins and pennies don't carry the same metaphor in Spanish. You need a completely different image.

examples.context: Someone finally understands the punchline of a joke.
examples.note: He fell/dropped — caer is used for understanding clicking. '¡Ya caí!' = I finally got it.

examples.context: After five minutes of explanation, they finally get it.
examples.note: 'It finally went in' — the information finally penetrated. Very colloquial.

examples.context: A student suddenly grasps a concept after weeks of confusion.
examples.note: Now I get it — pillar = to catch/get. Extremely common in Spain.

examples.context: Someone realises mid-conversation why you've been hinting.
examples.note: The lightbulb went on — same metaphor as English but different image. Used across Spain and Latin America.

examples.context: Finally understanding a complex instruction after a demo.
examples.note: Now I see it crystal clear — the moment of clarity expressed through vision.

title: not my circus not my monkeys
vibe: Cheerful detachment — not my problem, not my responsibility, I'm staying well out of it.
literal_fail: Interestingly, this phrase actually comes from Polish ('Nie mój cyrk, nie moje małpy'). Spaniards have their own equivalents.

examples.context: Colleagues arguing about something that doesn't involve you.
examples.note: That's not my business — clean, simple, the standard way to disengage.

examples.context: Drama in a friend group you're not part of.
examples.es: Yo no me meto en eso.
examples.note: I'm not getting involved in that — active choice to stay out, not just observation.

examples.context: Work chaos that belongs to another department.
examples.es: Eso lo tienen que resolver ellos.
examples.note: They need to sort that out themselves — assigns responsibility while removing yourself.

examples.context: Family drama you've wisely decided to avoid.
examples.note: 'Up to them' — short, final, beautifully detached. One of the most useful phrases in Spanish.

examples.context: Watching two friends argue while you sip your drink.
examples.note: Let them manage it themselves — apañarse is that Spanish verb for muddling through on your own.

title: you're having a laugh
vibe: British disbelief — you can't be serious, this is absurd, surely this is a joke.
literal_fail: 'Estás teniendo una risa' means nothing. Spanish expresses this with completely different constructions.

examples.context: A shop wants €50 for a sandwich.
examples.note: Are you joking? — the most direct Spanish equivalent. Deadpan delivery is key.

examples.context: The deadline has been moved to tomorrow.
examples.note: Are you pulling my leg? — slightly more personal, implies you think they're winding you up.

examples.context: Someone suggests a four-hour meeting.
examples.es: Esto no puede ser en serio.
examples.note: This can't be serious — calm, controlled disbelief.

examples.context: A parking fine for a spot that wasn't clearly marked.
examples.note: What a nerve/cheek — cara (face) used for audacity. Very Spanish expression of indignation.

examples.context: They've cancelled the event at the last minute again.
examples.note: What a joke — menudo/a + noun is the Spanish construction for 'what a [thing].' Sarcastic.

title: as luck would have it
vibe: Wry acknowledgement of coincidence — usually ironic, whether the luck was good or bad.
literal_fail: 'Como la suerte quiso' is too poetic and formal. Natural Spanish uses shorter, more spoken constructions.

examples.context: The one day you forget your umbrella, it pours.
examples.es: Como no podía ser de otra manera...
examples.note: 'As it couldn't have been otherwise' — resigned, slightly ironic. Perfect for bad luck.

examples.context: You bump into exactly the person you needed to see.
examples.es: Qué oportuno / da la casualidad de que...
examples.note: How timely — or the coincidence construction. Depends on tone: lucky vs ironic.

examples.context: The train is late on the one important day.
examples.es: Pues claro, el día que más prisa tenía.
examples.note: Of course, the day I was in most of a hurry — resigned Spanish black humour.

examples.context: Finding €20 in an old jacket when you're broke.
examples.note: Look at that luck — genuine or ironic depending on tone. Versatile.

examples.context: The one colleague who could help is on holiday.
examples.note: Of course, naturally — used ironically when something inconvenient is depressingly predictable.

title: hit the ground running
vibe: Starting something at full pace from the very first moment — no warming up, no easing in.
literal_fail: 'Golpear el suelo corriendo' sounds like you fell over. Spanish uses different metaphors for fast starts.

examples.context: A new employee who's already producing results in week one.
examples.es: Entró con todo desde el primer día.
examples.note: He came in with everything from day one — full commitment, no settling-in period.

examples.context: Launching a project at full speed immediately.
examples.note: We started at full throttle — machine/engine metaphors are common in Spanish for speed.

examples.context: Starting the new year with immediate action.
examples.es: Empezar el año con el pie derecho.
examples.note: Starting on the right foot — slightly different (doing it right vs doing it fast) but the closest idiom.

examples.context: A team that needs no warm-up period.
examples.es: Se pusieron las pilas desde el primer momento.
examples.note: 'They put their batteries in from the first moment' — got energised immediately.

examples.context: Diving straight into a new role after joining.
examples.note: He shot out from the start — disparado (fired like a bullet) captures the speed perfectly.

title: over the moon
vibe: Thrilled beyond words — used for genuine, exuberant joy about something that's gone brilliantly.
literal_fail: 'Sobre la luna' doesn't work. Spanish happiness uses completely different imagery — not moons.

examples.context: Your team just won the championship.
examples.es: Estamos contentísimos / estamos que no cabemos en nosotros mismos.
examples.note: 'We don't fit inside ourselves' — bursting with joy. More vivid than any moon.

examples.context: Getting the job you really wanted.
examples.note: Seventh heaven — the closest spatial metaphor to 'over the moon' in Spanish.

examples.context: A new parent hearing their baby's first word.
examples.note: Crazy with happiness — the intensity Spanish reaches for in moments of pure joy.

examples.context: Hearing your favourite band is touring again.
examples.note: It gave me enormous ilusión — ilusión means excited anticipation in Spanish, not illusion.

examples.context: Passing an exam you thought you'd failed.
examples.note: I got an enormous piece of joy — the Spanish construction for receiving great news.

title: it's gone pear-shaped
vibe: Something has gone wrong — plans have collapsed, things have deteriorated, it's all off the rails.
literal_fail: 'Se ha vuelto con forma de pera' is absurd. Spanish uses entirely different images for things falling apart.

examples.context: A project that was going well suddenly implodes.
examples.note: 'It all went to the draining board' — a mess, completely ruined. Very common.

examples.context: Holiday plans that collapse at the last minute.
examples.note: Everything twisted/went wrong — torcerse is the verb for plans going sideways.

examples.context: A relationship that started well and ended badly.
examples.note: Things got complicated — the understated Spanish version of a deteriorating situation.

examples.context: The event that was supposed to be perfect descends into chaos.
examples.es: Se montó un lío de mucho cuidado.
examples.note: A right mess kicked off — lío is the Spanish word for chaos, tangle, trouble.

examples.context: A business deal that fell through spectacularly.
examples.note: It went down (like a sinking ship) — pique = to sink. Perfect for total collapse.

title: by the skin of your teeth
vibe: Barely made it — survival or success achieved with the absolute minimum margin possible.
literal_fail: Teeth have skin in English (Job 19:20, King James Bible). Spanish doesn't use this image.

examples.context: Catching a train with literally ten seconds to spare.
examples.note: 'We caught it by the hairs' — por los pelos is the Spanish equivalent and it's perfect.

examples.context: Passing an exam with the minimum mark.
examples.note: Raspar = to scrape — passed by scraping through. Vivid and very common.

examples.context: Arriving at a meeting just as it starts.
examples.note: I arrived just in time — simple but effective. Add 'por los pelos' for drama.

examples.context: Finishing a project at the last possible second.
examples.note: The Latin phrase 'in extremis' is used in Spanish too — at the last possible moment.

examples.context: Getting the last seat on a sold-out flight.
examples.es: Me quedé con la última plaza por casualidad.
examples.note: I got the last place by luck — coincidence and barely-there margins together.

title: couldn't make it up
vibe: Said when reality is so strange or unfortunate that it sounds fictional — you'd never believe it if it weren't true.
literal_fail: 'No podrías inventarlo' is close but too passive. Spanish has more energetic ways of expressing this.

examples.context: Something absurdly improbable happening on the worst day.
examples.es: Parece de broma pero es verdad.
examples.note: It sounds like a joke but it's true — the most direct Spanish equivalent of this feeling.

examples.context: A series of coincidences too unlikely to be believable.
examples.es: Esto no me lo invento yo.
examples.note: 'I'm not making this up' — direct, indignant, very natural in storytelling.

examples.context: Describing a bizarre situation that actually happened.
examples.es: Si te lo cuento no te lo crees.
examples.note: If I told you you wouldn't believe it — classic storytelling opener in Spanish.

examples.context: Something going wrong in the most unlikely way.
examples.es: Solo a mí me pasa esto.
examples.note: 'Only to me does this happen' — Spanish for being spectacularly unlucky. Everyone relates.

examples.context: An unbelievably bad day described to friends.
examples.note: You have to see it to believe it — when the truth is stranger than fiction.

title: face like a smacked bottom
vibe: British for someone wearing a sour, miserable, or deeply unamused expression.
literal_fail: Translating this literally would be both wrong and alarming. Spanish has its own vivid face-based expressions.

examples.context: Someone sitting at a party looking thoroughly miserable.
examples.note: 'Face of few friends' — looking unfriendly, unapproachable, or deeply grumpy. Perfect.

examples.context: A colleague who looks furious after a meeting.
examples.note: 'Vinegar face' — sour, bitter expression. The Spanish equivalent hits just as hard.

examples.context: Someone tutting and sighing at everything.
examples.es: Está con una cara que no hay quien se le acerque.
examples.note: His face is such that no one can approach him — paints the picture vividly.

examples.context: A teenager who clearly doesn't want to be at the family dinner.
examples.note: Has a bad face — simple but effective. Can mean ill or just grumpy, context decides.

examples.context: Someone looking put-out after being told no.
examples.es: Se le cayó la cara al suelo.
examples.note: His face fell to the floor — different emotion (more disappointment) but equally vivid imagery.

title: bit much isn't it
vibe: Mild British understatement for something excessive, inappropriate, or over the top — delivered with quiet exasperation.
literal_fail: 'Un poco demasiado, ¿no?' works but sounds like a translation. Spanish understatement lands differently.

examples.context: Someone shows up two hours late without apologising.
examples.note: That's going too far — pasarse is the verb for overstepping a mark. Useful and very Spanish.

examples.context: A waiter who is borderline rude.
examples.note: A bit of respect, no? — quiet but pointed. The Spanish version of understated objection.

examples.context: Someone dominating every conversation at a dinner.
examples.note: That's enough, don't you think? — gentle but firm pushback on excess.

examples.context: A charge that seems excessive for a simple service.
examples.note: I think it's an abuse — stronger than 'bit much' but lands in the same territory.

examples.context: Someone going over the top with drama about a minor thing.
examples.note: It's not that big a deal — dismissing the excess with calm Spanish detachment.

title: blinding
vibe: British slang for something excellent — outstanding, brilliant, absolutely top-notch.
literal_fail: 'Cegador' means blinding literally and sounds alarming. Spanish cool/excellence has its own vocabulary.

examples.context: A goal scored from 30 yards that bends into the corner.
examples.note: Beastly — the Spanish equivalent of blinding for something jaw-droppingly good.

examples.context: A meal that's just phenomenally good.
examples.note: It's to die for — one of the strongest Spanish compliments for food. Delicious to the point of drama.

examples.context: A night out that goes better than expected.
examples.note: Brutal — used positively in Spanish slang, like blinding. Completely excellent.

examples.context: Someone who plays football at an extraordinary level.
examples.note: It's something else / it blows you away — pasada covers excellence that exceeds expectations.

examples.context: A piece of music that genuinely moves you.
examples.note: Mind-blowing — flipar is to be amazed, wowed, blown away. Very current Spanish slang.

title: she'll be right
vibe: Breezy, optimistic dismissal of worry — it'll be fine, don't stress, things have a way of working out.
literal_fail: 'Ella estará bien' sounds like you're worried about a specific woman. This is about situations, not people.

examples.context: Worrying about whether the plan will work out.
examples.note: 'It'll sort itself out' — the Spanish disposition toward things working out. Very natural.

examples.context: Friends fretting about being slightly late.
examples.note: Relax, nothing's going to happen — the great Spanish reassurance. Used constantly.

examples.context: Someone anxious about a minor problem.
examples.es: No te preocupes, eso tiene fácil arreglo.
examples.note: Don't worry, that's easily fixed — solving the problem by refusing to be bothered by it.

examples.context: Reassurance before a big presentation.
examples.es: Venga, que va a salir genial.
examples.note: Come on, it's going to go great — venga as an encourager, the Spanish 'come on.'

examples.context: Someone worried whether guests will enjoy the food.
examples.es: Que sí, que sí, no te agobies.
examples.note: Yes, yes, don't stress — agobiarse is to get overwhelmed by worry. Dismissing the anxiety.

title: dead cert
vibe: Absolute certainty — there's no doubt, this is guaranteed, bank on it.
literal_fail: 'Cierto muerto' means 'dead truth' which is nonsense. Spanish certainty uses different vocabulary.

examples.context: Predicting a result before a match.
examples.es: Es seguro como la muerte y los impuestos.
examples.note: As certain as death and taxes — the Spanish equivalent idiom. Dramatic but widely known.

examples.context: Knowing you'll get the job before the interview.
examples.note: 'It's sung' — already decided, a foregone conclusion. One of the most useful Spanish idioms.

examples.context: Knowing a horse will win before the race.
examples.note: A sure thing — pleno can mean a full win, a certainty. Betting language.

examples.context: Predicting a colleague will be chosen for the promotion.
examples.note: It's done — already decided, inevitable. Quiet confidence in the outcome.

examples.context: Someone is going to get in trouble — it's only a matter of when.
examples.es: Le va a caer una buena, seguro.
examples.note: He's going to get a good one, for sure — a punishment is certainly coming.

title: I'll give you that
vibe: Grudging concession — you disagree overall but acknowledge one specific point is fair. Debate culture staple.
literal_fail: 'Te lo daré' sounds like you're about to hand someone something. Spanish concession works differently.

examples.context: Admitting a rival team played well in defeat.
examples.es: Eso sí, en eso tienes razón.
examples.note: 'That yes, in that you're right' — eso sí is the Spanish verbal move for a targeted concession.

examples.context: Agreeing with one point in an argument you're losing.
examples.note: 'There I give you reason' — dar la razón is the Spanish phrase for conceding a point.

examples.context: Acknowledging a flaw in your own argument.
examples.note: On that, agreed — clipped, grudging, exactly the right tone.

examples.context: Admitting a competitor's product has one good feature.
examples.es: Hay que reconocer que en eso sí aciertan.
examples.note: You have to recognise that they get that right — reconocer (acknowledge) is the verb for grudging credit.

examples.context: Conceding a point to a sibling in a family argument.
examples.es: Vale, en eso puede que tengas razón.
examples.note: OK, on that you might be right — puede que softens it to a reluctant maybe.
